opus-5.5.text:
I think synthetic data plays quite different roles in the two cases, and the difference comes from where the bottleneck sits.

For language models, we started with an enormous amount of real data: essentially the whole internet, books, code, accumulated over decades. Pretraining could go a long way just by consuming that. Synthetic data came in later, mainly once the high-quality human text started running out, or when we wanted capabilities the internet doesn't cover well, like long chains of mathematical reasoning, careful step-by-step problem solving, or specific instruction-following formats. In that setting, synthetic data is more of a refinement and amplification tool. You already have a strong model, it generates candidates, and you filter them with verifiers, reward models, or execution results, like running the code to see if it passes. The key is that there's a reliable signal for what counts as good, so the model can bootstrap itself. Without that verification, you risk the model just recycling its own biases and collapsing.

Embodied intelligence is almost the opposite situation. There is no internet of robot data. Every trajectory of a real robot grasping, pushing, or folding something costs real time, real hardware, and often a human teleoperator. So from the very beginning, the data scale is orders of magnitude smaller than language. Synthetic data here isn't icing on the cake. It's closer to a foundation, or at least one of the main pillars, alongside real-world data and human video.

The forms are also different. In robotics, synthetic data mostly means simulation: physics engines, procedurally generated scenes, randomized object shapes, textures, lighting, and dynamics. Increasingly it also means using generative models, like video or world models, to imagine plausible interactions. The hard problem is the sim-to-real gap. Language is a closed symbolic system, so text generated by a model is the same kind of thing as text written by a person. Physical interaction isn't like that. Friction, contact, deformable objects, and sensor noise are very hard to simulate faithfully, so a policy that looks perfect in simulation can fail in a real kitchen.

So my view is roughly this. In language models, synthetic data's value is about going beyond human data: pushing reasoning and specialized skills further when the verification signal is clear. In embodied intelligence, its value is about making up for the absence of data: providing scale and diversity that the real world can't yet supply cheaply. But it has to be anchored by real-world data, because reality is ultimately the verifier. The most promising path, I think, is a pyramid: massive synthetic and video data at the bottom for broad priors, a smaller layer of real robot data to ground it in physics, and on top, real-world deployment and feedback that keeps correcting the model. Whoever builds the most efficient loop between those layers will probably make the biggest progress.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data became useful for language models as high-quality human text ran short, but it does not attribute synthetic data predominating in GPT-5 to exhaustion of internet data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that synthetic data plays almost opposite roles in those two worlds, and that difference tells you a lot about where each field actually is.

In language models, synthetic data arrived late and as a supplement. We'd already scraped most of the useful human-written text on the internet. The model learned the structure of language, facts, reasoning patterns from real human output. Synthetic data came in afterward to fill specific gaps: more math problems, more code with verified solutions, more instruction-following examples, more of a long-tail domain where humans just hadn't written enough. And critically, in a lot of these cases you have a verifier. A math answer is right or wrong. Code compiles and passes tests or it doesn't. So you can generate a huge volume, filter hard, and keep only what's correct. That's what makes synthetic data in language work as well as it does. The model is a bit like a student who's already read the whole library and is now doing targeted practice problems with an answer key.

Embodied intelligence is the reverse situation. There is no internet of robot trajectories. Nobody spent twenty years uploading billions of examples of a gripper picking up a cup from slightly different angles, with contact forces, with the cup half-full. The real data that exists is tiny, expensive, and tied to specific hardware. So synthetic data isn't the supplement there. For a lot of groups it's the main course. Simulation, procedural scene generation, domain randomization, world models that hallucinate futures. You're trying to manufacture the equivalent of the internet-scale corpus that language got for free.

But here's the catch, and it's why I don't think you can just copy the language playbook. In language, the generator and the target live in the same medium. Text generating text. The distribution gap is manageable. In robotics, the generator is a physics engine or a learned world model, and the target is the actual physical world. Friction, deformable objects, lighting, sensor noise, the way a cable actually behaves. Every one of those is a place where simulation lies to you a little, and those small lies compound when you execute a long sequence of actions. The sim-to-real gap is not a detail. It's the central problem.

And the verifier that saved language doesn't really exist. What's the "unit test" for a successful grasp in simulation? The simulator says it succeeded, but the simulator is the thing you don't trust. So you can't do the generate-and-filter loop with the same confidence.

So my framing is this. In language, synthetic data is about sharpening a model that already has a good prior from humans. In embodied intelligence, synthetic data is about bootstrapping a prior that doesn't exist yet, and then the real-world data, small as it is, becomes the precious thing you use to anchor and correct it. The ratio flips. Language is mostly real with synthetic on top. Embodied is mostly synthetic with real as the ground truth you're constantly calibrating against.

I'd add one thing that I think people underestimate. The reason synthetic data works at all in either domain is that it lets you control the distribution. You can decide to oversample the rare, dangerous, or boring cases that humans would never bother to record. For a robot, that's the dropped object, the occluded view, the near-collision. You're not just making more data, you're making data about what you want the model to be good at. That's the real value, and that part is shared across both fields.

astra-6.text:
I think synthetic data plays somewhat different roles in these two areas, although the underlying idea is the same: we want to create useful learning experiences beyond what we can collect directly.

For natural-language models, synthetic data can turn existing knowledge into material that is easier to learn from—questions and answers, worked examples, or different ways of expressing the same problem. It is particularly useful when we can check the result. For example, if we generate a programming problem and a solution, we can run the code. That feedback helps distinguish a useful example from something that merely sounds convincing.

The limitation is that generating more text does not automatically create more knowledge. If a model produces examples that repeat its own mistakes, training on them can reinforce those mistakes. So I would focus less on the volume of synthetic data and more on its diversity, how it is verified, and what capability it is intended to teach.

For embodied intelligence, synthetic data has an additional role: it lets a system practice interactions. A robot needs to learn how its actions change the world. In simulation, we can vary objects, lighting, friction, and obstacles, and let it attempt tasks that would be expensive or risky to repeat in reality.

But then the key question is whether what it learns transfers to the physical world. A simulator always leaves something out. A policy may succeed because it exploits a simplification in the simulation, and then fail on a real robot. So real-world observations and experiments remain essential for checking and improving the synthetic environment.

My view is that synthetic data is most valuable as part of a feedback loop: identify where the model fails, generate relevant experiences, verify them, train, and test again. For language models, verification often concerns whether an answer is correct. For embodied models, it also concerns whether an action actually works under physical constraints.

sol-6.1.text:
I think synthetic data plays a different role in these two settings, although the underlying idea is the same: use data we can generate and control to help a model learn things that are difficult to capture at sufficient scale in the real world.

For natural-language models, synthetic data is especially useful for making training more targeted. You can generate examples of a particular task, explore different ways of asking a question, or create problems with answers that can be checked. But generating more text doesn’t automatically create more knowledge. If the generator makes mistakes and those mistakes aren’t filtered out, you can end up reinforcing them. So the key is the quality of the feedback and verification, rather than simply the volume of generated data.

For embodied intelligence, synthetic data often means simulation: generating environments, objects, sensor observations, and interactions. That’s valuable because collecting real-world interaction data can be slow and expensive. In simulation, you can repeat an experiment, vary the conditions, and expose a model to situations that would be difficult to arrange physically.

The challenge there is whether what the model learns transfers to the real world. A simulated environment can look convincing and still behave differently in ways that matter for control. So I would see synthetic data and real data as complementary: simulation gives you scale and controlled variation, while real-world experience tells you where your assumptions are wrong.

In both cases, the important question is: what capability does this data actually teach, and how do we verify that the capability works outside the data-generation process?
